- When sentiment is high (≥0.3) and forecast shows a sharp upward move, reduce the peak by 5–10% to avoid overshoot.  
- If sentiment is low (≤0.1) and forecast is trending down, avoid excessive downward correction — allow slight mean reversion but don’t overcorrect.  
- After a recent spike in price, forecast should show a slight downward bias (−2 to −5%) in the next 3–5 days to reflect mean reversion.  
- If sentiment is rising (e.g., 0.27–0.53) and forecast is flat or declining, adjust upward by 2–5% to capture sentiment-driven momentum.  
- For 30-day horizon, avoid overfitting to recent highs — if last 3–5 days are trending down, forecast should not dip below 10% below recent low.  
- When sentiment is volatile (alternating 0.00–0.53), use a smoothing filter — don’t let forecast swing more than 3% from prior day’s value.  
- If true outcome is consistently below forecast (e.g., 5–10% gap), check sentiment for overconfidence — reduce forecast by 3–7% if sentiment is >0.4.  
- If sentiment is low and forecast is high, consider a “sentiment lag” correction — delay peak by 1–2 days and reduce amplitude by 5–10%.
